articles.title: NestJS API Quota Management: meet nestjs-quota
articles.excerpt: If you run a multi-tenant API on NestJS, you probably need more than a rate limiter. You need to answer "may this request proceed?" against several limits at once (per user per minute, per tenant per…
articles.body: If you run a multi-tenant API on NestJS, you probably need more than a rate limiter. You need to answer "may this request proceed?" against several limits at once (per user per minute, per tenant per day, per tenant per month) and "how much has each tenant actually used?" for billing and dashboards. nest-quota is an open-source package that does both. It checks and consumes all the relevant quotas in one atomic operation, so you never end up with a half-charged request. It works across multiple servers using a single Redis Lua script per decision. It supports idempotent retries, reserve/commit/release for operations whose cost you don't know up front, plan-based dynamic limits, and configurable fail-open or fail-closed behavior.

articles.title: Six ${VAR} forms, five .mcp.json fields, two tiny servers: what Claude Code MCP expansion actually produced
articles.excerpt: I put six environment-variable forms into the args, env and command fields of one project .mcp.json (plus url and headers on a second, HTTP server) and read back what the server process actually recei…
articles.body: I put six environment-variable forms into the args , env and command fields of one project .mcp.json (plus url and headers on a second, HTTP server) and read back what the server process actually received. On Claude Code 2.1.278, ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expanded everywhere, $VAR never expanded anywhere, an unset ${VAR} arrived as the literal text, and a nested ${A:-${B}} expanded only in headers because that field is expanded twice. The MCP page in the Claude Code docs says two syntaxes are supported and five fields are expanded. That leaves a lot unsaid: what happens to a bare $VAR , to a nested default, to a variable that is unset, and whether all five fields behave the same.

articles.title: Fable 5.1 costs twice as much as Opus 5, until your cache gets big enough
articles.excerpt: Claude Fable 5.1 shipped on September 1 with the same $10 input / $50 output per million tokens as Fable 5. One number moved: cache reads dropped from $1 to $0.25 per million. On the price sheet it st…
articles.body: Claude Fable 5.1 shipped on September 1 with the same $10 input / $50 output per million tokens as Fable 5. One number moved: cache reads dropped from $1 to $0.25 per million. On the price sheet it still costs twice what Opus 5 does ($5 / $25). But look at the cache-read column and the order flips. Fable 5.1 charges $0.25 there, Opus 5 charges $0.50. So which one is cheaper depends on how much of each request is served from cache, and I wanted the actual crossover instead of a vibe. A request bill has three parts Cached tokens times the cache-read price, fresh input times the input price, output times the output price. Fable 5.1 only changed the first term, so the saving over Fable 5 is exactly as big as that term's share of your bill.

articles.title: What Makes a Coding Agent Trustworthy? A Look at SolonCode's Design Choices
articles.excerpt: Every week there's a new coding agent, and every week someone asks the same question in a slightly different tone: can I actually trust this thing with my codebase? It's a fair question. A coding agen…
articles.body: Every week there's a new coding agent, and every week someone asks the same question in a slightly different tone: can I actually trust this thing with my codebase? It's a fair question. A coding agent reads your source, runs commands in your shell, and — increasingly — edits files and opens pull requests on its own. That's a lot of access to hand to a black box. So instead of arguing about which agent is "smartest," I want to talk about a less glamorous property: trust . What does it actually take for a coding agent to earn it? I'll use SolonCode — an open-source coding agent built in Java on top of Solon AI — as a concrete reference, not because it's the only good answer, but because its design happens to line up with a checklist I think is worth having.

articles.excerpt: Short answer: building an MCP-compatible client for AI agents is 20% protocol and 80% OpenClaw, Hermes) wants params before validation, and stay stateless for clients that never initialize. mcp client…
articles.body: Short answer: building an MCP-compatible client for AI agents is 20% protocol and 80% edge-case handling. Each client (Cursor, Claude Desktop, Windsurf, OpenClaw , Hermes) wants a slightly different JSON shape for the same Streamable HTTP server; the only way to keep one server working across all of them is to generate that shape per platform, pin the single upstream URL in one place, forward exactly two headers deliberately, normalise non-object JSON-RPC params before validation, and stay stateless for clients that never send initialize . mcp client is searched about 1,600 times a month; almost none of those readers need the specification - they need the config that does not 401. Key takeaways One server, one upstream string.

articles.title: Trimming Video in the Browser: Why "Precise" and "Fast" Give Different Cuts
articles.excerpt: There are two ways to cut a clip, and they answer different questions. A precise cut re-encodes the video, so the cut lands on exactly the frame you chose. A fast cut copies the compressed stream with…
articles.body: There are two ways to cut a clip, and they answer different questions. A precise cut re-encodes the video, so the cut lands on exactly the frame you chose. A fast cut copies the compressed stream without decoding it, so the cut snaps to the nearest keyframe and the start can shift. Neither approach is wrong. Each is a trade between accuracy and speed. The rest of this post explains why, with the actual ffmpeg commands for both. Why a cut cannot always be arbitrary Video is not stored as a sequence of independent frames. Most frames are described relative to other frames. A keyframe, also called an I-frame, is self-contained: it can be decoded on its own. The frames after it carry only the differences. The stretch from one keyframe to the next is a GOP, a group of pictures.

articles.body: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, recently completed a rigorous series of environmental and physical tests on a new small satellite designed to make spaceflight safer and more efficient. The ASCENT (Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic) Propulsion Dual Mode mission is a flight demonstration of a spacecraft about the size of a large shoebox.
